claim: Connections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) regulate memory and emotion.
source: Connections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) regulate memory and emotion and become disrupted in neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Etkin et al., 2011) as indicated in the introduction.

claim: Connections from the BLA to PFC become disrupted in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Connections from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) regulate memory and emotion and become disrupted in neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Gilboa et al., 2004; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016; McTeague et al., 2020) as indicated in the introduction.

claim: The rostral BLA (rBLA) and caudal BLA (cBLA) differentially project to prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions of the mouse PFC.
source: To examine these circuits, we first used retrograde and anterograde anatomy to show that the rostral BLA (rBLA) and caudal BLA (cBLA) differentially project to prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions of the mouse PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde and anterograde anatomical tracing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: rBLA preferentially drives layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons in PL.
source: Using ex vivo whole-cell recordings and optogenetics, we then assessed which neuronal subtypes are targeted, showing that rBLA preferentially drives layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons in PL, whereas cBLA drives layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons in IL.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data combined with optogenetic stimulation shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: cBLA drives layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons in IL.
source: Using ex vivo whole-cell recordings and optogenetics, we then assessed which neuronal subtypes are targeted, showing that rBLA preferentially drives layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons in PL, whereas cBLA drives layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons in IL.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data combined with optogenetic stimulation shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: cBLA mainly influences IL L5 in vivo.
source: We next combined in vivo silicon probe recordings and optogenetics to confirm that cBLA mainly influences IL L5, whereas rBLA primarily activates PL L2, but also evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Neuropixels recordings with optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4.

claim: rBLA primarily activates PL L2 in vivo.
source: We next combined in vivo silicon probe recordings and optogenetics to confirm that cBLA mainly influences IL L5, whereas rBLA primarily activates PL L2, but also evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Neuropixels recordings with optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4.

claim: rBLA evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
source: We next combined in vivo silicon probe recordings and optogenetics to confirm that cBLA mainly influences IL L5, whereas rBLA primarily activates PL L2, but also evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4 and ex vivo recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: rBLA can engage L2 CA neurons to impact L5 PT neuron activity.
source: Lastly, we used soma-tagged optogenetics to explore the local circuits linking superficial and deep layers of PL, showing how rBLA can engage L2 CA neurons to impact L5 PT neuron activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by soma-tagged optogenetics experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC.
source: The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC, which contact specific cell types to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas (Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Little and Carter, 2013; Cheriyan et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BLA inputs contact specific cell types in the PFC to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas.
source: The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC, which contact specific cell types to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas (Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Little and Carter, 2013; Cheriyan et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The PFC is subdivided along the dorsoventral axis into the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions.
source: The PFC is subdivided along the dorsoventral axis into the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions (Van De Werd et al., 2010; Van De Werd and Uylings, 2014), which play different functional roles in behavioral paradigms like threat conditioning (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PL and IL play different functional roles in behavioral paradigms like threat conditioning.
source: The PFC is subdivided along the dorsoventral axis into the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions (Van De Werd et al., 2010; Van De Werd and Uylings, 2014), which play different functional roles in behavioral paradigms like threat conditioning (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The BLA is subdivided along the rostro-caudal axis into anterior (magnocellular) and posterior (parvocellular) regions.
source: Similarly, the BLA is subdivided along the rostro-caudal axis into anterior (magnocellular) and posterior (parvocellular) regions (McDonald, 2003; O'Leary et al., 2020), which also play distinct roles in aversive and appetitive behaviors (Kim et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anterior and posterior regions of the BLA play distinct roles in aversive and appetitive behaviors.
source: Similarly, the BLA is subdivided along the rostro-caudal axis into anterior (magnocellular) and posterior (parvocellular) regions (McDonald, 2003; O'Leary et al., 2020), which also play distinct roles in aversive and appetitive behaviors (Kim et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One population of cells in anterior BLA targets PL, while a separate group in posterior BLA targets IL.
source: Anatomical studies using transgenic mice suggest one population of cells in anterior BLA targets PL, while a separate group in posterior BLA targets IL (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There are multiple projections from cells distributed along the rostral to caudal axis of the BLA.
source: However, recent work suggests a more complicated relationship, with multiple projections from cells distributed along the rostral to caudal axis of the BLA (Hintiryan et al., 2021), which have an unknown influence on activity and output of the PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: BLA inputs to PL target layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons.
source: BLA inputs to PL target layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons, which in turn project back to the BLA, forming a direct, reciprocal circuit under the control of local inhibition (Little and Carter, 2013; McGarry and Carter, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PL L2 CA neurons project back to the BLA, forming a direct, reciprocal circuit under the control of local inhibition.
source: BLA inputs to PL target layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons, which in turn project back to the BLA, forming a direct, reciprocal circuit under the control of local inhibition (Little and Carter, 2013; McGarry and Carter, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BLA connections in IL can activate layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons.
source: In contrast, BLA connections in IL can activate layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brain regions to exert top-down control of behavior (Cheriyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IL L5 PT neurons project to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brain regions to exert top-down control of behavior.
source: In contrast, BLA connections in IL can activate layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brain regions to exert top-down control of behavior (Cheriyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Largely separate populations of PL and IL-projecting neurons exist across the BLA.
source: We observed largely separate populations of PL and IL-projecting neurons across the BLA, with a smaller population of dual-projection neurons (PL = 583 ± 59 cells, IL = 694 ± 78 cells, dual = 246 ± 30 cells, n = 3 animals) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PL-projecting neurons are biased toward the rostral BLA (rBLA).
source: Labeled cells were distributed along a gradient in the rostro-caudal axis, with PL-projecting neurons biased toward the rostral BLA (rBLA), and IL-projecting neurons shifted toward the cBLA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IL-projecting neurons are shifted toward the cBLA.
source: Labeled cells were distributed along a gradient in the rostro-caudal axis, with PL-projecting neurons biased toward the rostral BLA (rBLA), and IL-projecting neurons shifted toward the cBLA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1C.

claim: rBLA axons are primarily in PL and cBLA axons are in IL.
source: Consistent with our retrograde labeling, we observed rBLA axons primarily in PL and cBLA axons in IL, with distinct laminar targeting in each subregion (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1E.

claim: rBLA primarily targets PL L2.
source: Quantifying axon fluorescence across layers and subregions established that rBLA primarily targeted PL L2, whereas cBLA targeted IL L5 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1F.

claim: cBLA targets IL L5.
source: Quantifying axon fluorescence across layers and subregions established that rBLA primarily targeted PL L2, whereas cBLA targeted IL L5 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1F.

claim: rBLA-evoked EPSCs are much larger at PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L2 CA, PL L5 PT, and IL L5 PT neurons.
source: Taking this approach, we observed that rBLA-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at −60 mV were much larger at PL L2 CA neurons compared to all other cell types in the different layers and subregions (EPSC ratio: IL L2 CA vs. PL L2 CA = 0.03, geometric standard deviation factor [GSD] = 12.3, p = 0.0003; n = 8 pairs; PL L5 PT vs. PL L2 CA = 0.02, GSD = 2.6, p = 0.0001; n = 8 pairs; IL L5 PT vs. PL L2 CA = 0.09, GSD = 7.7, p = 0.006; n = 8 pairs; 5 animals) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 2C.

claim: cBLA-evoked EPSCs are much larger at IL L5 PT neurons compared to PL L2 CA, IL L2 CA, and PL L5 PT neurons.
source: In contrast, cBLA-evoked EPSCs were much larger at IL L5 PT neurons compared to all other cell types (EPSC ratio: PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT = 0.06, GSD = 9.3, p = 0.005; n = 7 pairs; IL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT = 0.11, GSD = 10.5, p = 0.014; n = 7 pairs; PL L5 PT vs. IL L5 PT = 0.008, GSD = 3.1, p < 0.0001; n = 8 pairs; 6 animals) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 2D.

claim: rBLA and cBLA primarily make connections close to the soma of pyramidal neurons in the PFC.
source: We found strong rBLA and cBLA input to the basal and perisomatic dendrites of PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons, respectively, and no rBLA input to either the apical or basal dendrites of PL L5 PT neurons (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from subcellular channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping (sCRACM) shown in Figure 2F.

claim: rBLA does not target the apical or basal dendrites of PL L5 PT neurons.
source: We found strong rBLA and cBLA input to the basal and perisomatic dendrites of PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons, respectively, and no rBLA input to either the apical or basal dendrites of PL L5 PT neurons (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sCRACM shown in Figure 2F.

claim: rBLA-evoked EPSCs are largest at PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L5 PT neurons.
source: We found that rBLA-evoked EPSCs were again largest at PL L2 CA neurons (EPSC1: PL L2 CA = −401 ± 63 pA; IL L5 PT = −133 ± 55 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0078, n = 8 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claim: rBLA-evoked IPSCs are of comparable amplitude at PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons.
source: In contrast, rBLA-evoked IPSCs were of comparable amplitude at PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons (IPSC1: PL L2 CA = 450 ± 86 pA; IL L5 PT = 521 ± 136 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.8125, n = 7 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claim: rBLA inputs onto PL L2 CA neurons show higher E/I ratios than IL L5 PT neurons.
source: We found differences in excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratios, with rBLA inputs onto PL L2 CA neurons showing higher values than IL L5 PT neurons (rBLA E/I ratio: PL L2 CA = 0.99, GSD = 1.9; IL L5 PT = 0.15, GSD = 2.7; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0156, n = 7 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claim: cBLA-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs are strongly biased onto IL L5 PT neurons compared to PL L2 CA neurons.
source: We found that both EPSCs and IPSCs were strongly biased onto IL L5 PT neurons (EPSC1: PL L2 CA = −31 ± 10 pA; IL L5 PT = −415 ± 139 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0156, n = 7 pairs, 4 animals) (IPSC1: PL L2 CA = 31 ± 28 pA; IL L5 PT = 858 ± 149 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0156, n = 7 pairs, 4 animals) (cBLA E/I ratio; IL L5 PT = 0.4, GSD = 2.3; n = 7 pairs, 4 animals) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3D.

claim: rBLA inputs evoke significantly more action potential firing of PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L5 PT neurons.
source: We found that rBLA inputs evoked significantly more action potential firing of PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L5 PT neurons in the same slices (firing probability: PL L2 CA = 0.88 ± 0.05, IL L5 PT = 0.23 ± 0.15, p = 0.016; n = 8 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3E.

claim: cBLA inputs activate only IL L5 PT neurons and never activate PL L2 CA neurons.
source: In contrast, cBLA inputs activated only IL L5 PT neurons and never activated PL L2 CA neurons (firing probability: PL L2 CA = 0, IL L5 PT = 0.98 ± 0.02, p = 0.03; n = 7 pairs, 3 animals) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3F.

claim: rBLA stimulation leads to more responsive units in PL L2, PL L5, and IL L5 compared to IL L2.
source: rBLA stimulation led to more responsive units in PL L2, PL L5, and IL L5 compared to IL L2 (PL L2 = 20.1%; IL L2 = 9.8%; PL L5 = 20.0%; IL L5 = 23.9% of single units in subregion), whereas cBLA stimulation mainly drove responses in IL L5 (PL L2 = 2.6%; IL L2 = 7.5%; PL L5 = 12.9%; IL L5 = 26.6% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: cBLA stimulation mainly drives responses in IL L5.
source: rBLA stimulation led to more responsive units in PL L2, PL L5, and IL L5 compared to IL L2 (PL L2 = 20.1%; IL L2 = 9.8%; PL L5 = 20.0%; IL L5 = 23.9% of single units in subregion), whereas cBLA stimulation mainly drove responses in IL L5 (PL L2 = 2.6%; IL L2 = 7.5%; PL L5 = 12.9%; IL L5 = 26.6% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The highest proportion of rBLA-activated units are found in PL L2.
source: The highest proportion of rBLA-activated units were found in PL L2 (PL L2 = 18.2%; IL L2 = 5.5%; PL L5 = 7.9%; IL L5 = 9.9% of single units in subregion), whereas rBLA-suppressed units were enriched in L5 of PL and IL (PL L2 = 1.9%; IL L2 = 4.3%; PL L5 = 12.4%; IL L5 = 14% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claim: rBLA-suppressed units are enriched in L5 of PL and IL.
source: The highest proportion of rBLA-activated units were found in PL L2 (PL L2 = 18.2%; IL L2 = 5.5%; PL L5 = 7.9%; IL L5 = 9.9% of single units in subregion), whereas rBLA-suppressed units were enriched in L5 of PL and IL (PL L2 = 1.9%; IL L2 = 4.3%; PL L5 = 12.4%; IL L5 = 14% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claim: cBLA-activated units are greatest in IL L5.
source: In contrast, cBLA-activated units were greatest in IL L5 (PL L2 = 1.3%; IL L2 = 5%; PL L5 = 4%; IL L5 = 17.7% of single units in subregion), with no significant differences in the proportion of cBLA-suppressed units (PL L2 = 1.3%; IL L2 = 2.5%; PL L5 = 8.9%; IL L5 = 8.9% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4G.

claim: rBLA evokes robust responses at PL L5 PT neurons at suprathreshold intensities but not at subthreshold intensities.
source: We found no responses at subthreshold intensities, but robust responses at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity from L2 to L5 is involved in rBLA-evoked responses at PL L5 PT neurons (EPSC: sub = −9 ± 4 pA, supra = −113 ± 24 pA, p = 0.02; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = 17 ± 5 pA, supra = 508 ± 101 pA, p = 0.008; n = 8 pairs; 4 animals) (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Polysynaptic activity from L2 to L5 is involved in rBLA-evoked responses at PL L5 PT neurons.
source: We found no responses at subthreshold intensities, but robust responses at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity from L2 to L5 is involved in rBLA-evoked responses at PL L5 PT neurons (EPSC: sub = −9 ± 4 pA, supra = −113 ± 24 pA, p = 0.02; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = 17 ± 5 pA, supra = 508 ± 101 pA, p = 0.008; n = 8 pairs; 4 animals) (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5B and 5C, and by inference from the lack of monosynaptic connections.

claim: rBLA does not evoke responses in IL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities.
source: In contrast, we observed no responses in IL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, suggesting activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 in the slice, and that rBLA instead projects directly to IL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 3 pA, supra = −7 ± 4 pA, p = 0.055; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = −7 ± 2 pA, supra = −11 ± 3 pA, p = 0.64; n = 8 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 in the slice.
source: In contrast, we observed no responses in IL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, suggesting activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 in the slice, and that rBLA instead projects directly to IL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 3 pA, supra = −7 ± 4 pA, p = 0.055; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = −7 ± 2 pA, supra = −11 ± 3 pA, p = 0.64; n = 8 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5D-F and by inference from the lack of responses.

claim: cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5.
source: In order to confirm that cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5, we also activated cBLA inputs in IL L5, and observed no EPSCs in PL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, and only minimal IPSCs at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity also does not spread from IL L5 to PL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 2 pA, supra = −13 ± 5 pA, p = 0.055; n = 9 pairs; IPSC: sub = 7 ± 2 pA, supra = 54 ± 22 pA, p = 0.027; n = 9 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: Polysynaptic activity does not spread from IL L5 to PL L5.
source: In order to confirm that cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5, we also activated cBLA inputs in IL L5, and observed no EPSCs in PL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, and only minimal IPSCs at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity also does not spread from IL L5 to PL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 2 pA, supra = −13 ± 5 pA, p = 0.055; n = 9 pairs; IPSC: sub = 7 ± 2 pA, supra = 54 ± 22 pA, p = 0.027; n = 9 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5G-I and by inference from the lack of responses.

claim: L2 stimulation can exclusively drive L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons.
source: We found that L2 stimulation could exclusively drive L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons, whereas L5 stimulation could drive L5 CA neurons without engaging L2 CA neurons, demonstrating restricted layer-specific activation (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: L5 stimulation can drive L5 CA neurons without engaging L2 CA neurons.
source: We found that L2 stimulation could exclusively drive L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons, whereas L5 stimulation could drive L5 CA neurons without engaging L2 CA neurons, demonstrating restricted layer-specific activation (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: PL L2 CA neurons evoke prominent EPSCs at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, but minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We found prominent EPSCs at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, but minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons (EPSC: L2 Pyr = −61 ± 19 pA, L3 Pyr = –13 ± 3 pA, L5 Pyr = −237 ± 96 pA; L2 vs. L3, p = 0.0373; L3 vs. L5, p = 0.0014; n = 8 triplets; 4 animals) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PL L2 CA neurons evoke prominent inhibition at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, with minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We also observed prominent inhibition at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, again with minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons (IPSC: L2 Pyr = 888 ± 263 pA, L3 Pyr = 80 ± 56 pA, L5 Pyr = 449 ± 236 pA; L2 vs. L3, p = 0.0014; n = 8 triplets; 4 animals) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6F.

claim: L5 pyramidal neurons have a significantly higher E/I ratio compared to L2 and L3 pyramidal neurons.
source: The overall effect was a significantly higher E/I ratio at L5 pyramidal neurons compared to the other cell types (E/I ratio: L2 Pyr = 0.06, GSD = 1.8, L3 Pyr = 0.36, GSD = 5.5, L5 Pyr = 0.8, GSD = 2.8; L2 vs. L5, p = 0.0059; n = 7 L2, 5 L3, and 8 L5 cells; 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics.

claim: PL L2 CA-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs are strongly biased onto L5 PT neurons compared to neighboring L5 IT neurons.
source: We observed robust PL L2 CA-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs, which were strongly biased onto L5 PT neurons compared to neighboring L5 IT neurons (EPSC: PL L5 PT = −67 ± 15 pA, PL L5 IT = −4 ± 1 pA, p = 0.0005; n = 12 pairs; 7 animals; IPSC: PL L5 PT = 229 ± 92 pA, PL L5 IT = 20 ± 15 pA, p = 0.03; n = 10 pairs; 6 animals) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Excitatory conductances alone evoke robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons.
source: We found that excitatory conductances alone evoked robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons, whereas injecting excitatory and inhibitory conductances resulted in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons (spikes per stimulus: PT E = 6.82 ± 0.54; PT E + I = 1.07 ± 0.49; IT E = 0 ± 0; IT E + I = 0 ± 0; n = 7 for each cell type, 4 animals) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Injecting excitatory and inhibitory conductances results in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons.
source: We found that excitatory conductances alone evoked robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons, whereas injecting excitatory and inhibitory conductances resulted in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons (spikes per stimulus: PT E = 6.82 ± 0.54; PT E + I = 1.07 ± 0.49; IT E = 0 ± 0; IT E + I = 0 ± 0; n = 7 for each cell type, 4 animals) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Activation of PL L2 CA neurons drives PL L5 PT spiking, but this can be strongly regulated by local inhibitory circuits.
source: These results indicate that activation of PL L2 CA neurons drives PL L5 PT spiking, but this can be strongly regulated by local inhibitory circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7D and by inference from the E/I balance experiments.

claim: rBLA primarily projects to PL and cBLA mostly projects to IL, indicating distinct connections.
source: We first use anatomy to show that rBLA primarily projects to PL, and cBLA mostly projects to IL, indicating distinct connections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde and anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1.

claim: rBLA preferentially activates PL L2 CA neurons and cBLA engages IL L5 PT neurons.
source: We next use ex vivo recordings and optogenetics to assess cell type-specific connections, showing that rBLA preferentially activates PL L2 CA neurons and cBLA engages IL L5 PT neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: cBLA influences are restricted to IL L5.
source: We then combine in vivo recordings with optogenetics and find that while cBLA influences are restricted to IL L5, rBLA drives both PL L2 and evokes robust polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: rBLA drives both PL L2 and evokes robust polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
source: We then combine in vivo recordings with optogenetics and find that while cBLA influences are restricted to IL L5, rBLA drives both PL L2 and evokes robust polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4 and ex vivo recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: PL L2 CA neurons mediate polysynaptic responses at PL L5 PT neurons.
source: Lastly, using soma-tagged optogenetics, we establish that this local influence reflects connections from PL L2 CA neurons onto PL L5 PT neurons within PL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Dysfunction of BLA-PFC connections contributes to neuropsychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and autism.
source: Dysfunction of these connections contributes to neuropsychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and autism (Gilboa et al., 2004; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016; McTeague et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Long-range inputs often make targeted connections onto specific cell types in the PFC.
source: In addition to contacting different subregions and layers, long-range inputs often make targeted connections onto specific cell types in the PFC (Anastasiades and Carter, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In motor cortex, layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons project to deeper layers and target L5 pyramidal neurons.
source: In motor cortex, layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons project to deeper layers and target L5 pyramidal neurons (Anderson et al., 2010; Hirai et al., 2012), whereas L5 PT neurons predominantly target nearby L5 PT neurons (Morishima and Kawaguchi, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: L5 PT neurons predominantly target nearby L5 PT neurons.
source: In motor cortex, layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons project to deeper layers and target L5 pyramidal neurons (Anderson et al., 2010; Hirai et al., 2012), whereas L5 PT neurons predominantly target nearby L5 PT neurons (Morishima and Kawaguchi, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PL-projecting neurons in rBLA and IL-projecting neurons in cBLA do not collateralize within PFC.
source: We again found that rBLA axons were prominent in PL L2 while cBLA axons were strongest in IL L5, consistent with our other anatomy and establishing that PL-projecting neurons in rBLA and IL-projecting neurons in cBLA do not collateralize within PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde-Cre experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: rBLA and cBLA are responsible for engaging different cell types in the PFC.
source: We next used whole-cell recordings and optogenetics to test whether rBLA and cBLA are responsible for engaging these different cell types in the PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: rBLA inputs target PL L2 CA neurons over L2 cortico-cortical (CC) neurons and IL L5 CA neurons.
source: In separate experiments, we also confirmed that rBLA inputs target PL L2 CA neurons over L2 cortico-cortical (CC) neurons and IL L5 CA neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and that cBLA inputs target IL L5 PT over IL L5 CA neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous results on non-specific BLA inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: cBLA inputs target IL L5 PT over IL L5 CA neurons.
source: In separate experiments, we also confirmed that rBLA inputs target PL L2 CA neurons over L2 cortico-cortical (CC) neurons and IL L5 CA neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and that cBLA inputs target IL L5 PT over IL L5 CA neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous results on non-specific BLA inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: rBLA and cBLA primarily make connections close to the soma of pyramidal neurons in the PFC, and do not target the apical dendrites of deep layer neurons.
source: Together, these findings indicate that rBLA and cBLA primarily make connections close to the soma of pyramidal neurons in the PFC, and do not target the apical dendrites of deep layer neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sCRACM shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: rBLA and cBLA directly excite their targets and evoke feed-forward inhibition that could prevent firing of action potentials.
source: These results show that rBLA and cBLA directly excite their targets and evoke feed-forward inhibition that could prevent firing of action potentials (APs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3 and by inference from the E/I balance.

claim: rBLA and cBLA engage distinct projection neuron networks in the PFC.
source: Together, these findings indicate rBLA and cBLA engage distinct projection neuron networks in the PFC, supporting the hypothesis that BLA consists of functionally distinct rostral and caudal divisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3.

claim: BLA consists of functionally distinct rostral and caudal divisions.
source: Together, these findings indicate rBLA and cBLA engage distinct projection neuron networks in the PFC, supporting the hypothesis that BLA consists of functionally distinct rostral and caudal divisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3 and by inference from the distinct connectivity patterns.

claim: rBLA and cBLA drive distinct activity in PL and IL.
source: Together, these findings indicate that rBLA and cBLA drive distinct activity in PL and IL, with rBLA primarily activating PL L2, but also unexpectedly generating mixed activation and suppression across L5, and cBLA predominantly activating IL L5, with few responses elsewhere.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: rBLA primarily activates PL L2, but also generates mixed activation and suppression across L5.
source: Together, these findings indicate that rBLA and cBLA drive distinct activity in PL and IL, with rBLA primarily activating PL L2, but also unexpectedly generating mixed activation and suppression across L5, and cBLA predominantly activating IL L5, with few responses elsewhere.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: cBLA predominantly activates IL L5, with few responses elsewhere.
source: Together, these findings indicate that rBLA and cBLA drive distinct activity in PL and IL, with rBLA primarily activating PL L2, but also unexpectedly generating mixed activation and suppression across L5, and cBLA predominantly activating IL L5, with few responses elsewhere.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: PL L2 CA neurons can mediate polysynaptic responses to rBLA inputs, leading to robust excitation and inhibition in deeper layers of the PFC.
source: Together, these recordings suggest that PL L2 CA neurons can mediate polysynaptic responses to rBLA inputs, leading to robust excitation and inhibition in deeper layers of the PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6.

claim: PL L2 CA neurons serve as a crucial node in a disynaptic feedforward circuit, which links rBLA input specifically to PL L5 PT neurons without significant input to L3 or other L5 neurons.
source: Together, these findings indicate that PL L2 CA neurons serve as a crucial node in a disynaptic feedforward circuit, which links rBLA input specifically to PL L5 PT neurons without significant input to L3 or other L5 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The influence of rBLA on PFC output will depend on the neuromodulatory state, which may alter the tightly balanced CA-evoked excitation and inhibition onto PL L5 PT neurons.
source: Consequently, the influence of rBLA on PFC output will depend on the neuromodulatory state, which may alter the tightly balanced CA-evoked excitation and inhibition onto PL L5 PT neurons (Floresco and Tse, 2007; Vander Weele et al., 2018; Anastasiades et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and by inference from the E/I balance experiments.

claim: rBLA participates in a rare example of a closed reciprocal loop with PL, contacting L2 CA neurons that in turn project back to the rBLA.
source: Our results confirm that rBLA participates in a rare example of a closed reciprocal loop with PL, contacting L2 CA neurons that in turn project back to the rBLA (Little and Carter, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and by experimental data from the current study.

claim: cBLA does not participate in a closed or open reciprocal loop with IL, instead making unidirectional connections onto L5 PT neurons.
source: In contrast, cBLA does not participate in a closed or open reciprocal loop with IL, instead making unidirectional connections onto L5 PT neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: BLA to PL projections are necessary for expression of threat conditioning.
source: For example, BLA to PL projections are necessary for expression of threat conditioning (Senn et al., 2014; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017), and because rBLA is the main input to PL, our findings are consistent with the rBLA playing a key role in aversion (Kim et al., 2016; Pi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: rBLA plays a key role in aversion.
source: For example, BLA to PL projections are necessary for expression of threat conditioning (Senn et al., 2014; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017), and because rBLA is the main input to PL, our findings are consistent with the rBLA playing a key role in aversion (Kim et al., 2016; Pi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and by inference from the current study's findings.

claim: BLA to IL projections are involved in the extinction of threat conditioning.
source: In contrast, BLA to IL projections are involved in the extinction of threat conditioning (Senn et al., 2014; Klavir et al., 2017), and because cBLA is the primary input to IL, our findings are also consistent with cBLA being involved in this learning (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: cBLA is involved in extinction learning.
source: In contrast, BLA to IL projections are involved in the extinction of threat conditioning (Senn et al., 2014; Klavir et al., 2017), and because cBLA is the primary input to IL, our findings are also consistent with cBLA being involved in this learning (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and by inference from the current study's findings.

claim: There are neurons that encode both positive and negative valence within the rBLA.
source: Further complicating this model of BLA function is recent work suggesting that there are neurons that encode both positive and negative valence within the rBLA (Zhang et al., 2021), which means both PL and IL could receive signals encoding positive and negative valence from different sources in the BLA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both PL and IL could receive signals encoding positive and negative valence from different sources in the BLA.
source: Further complicating this model of BLA function is recent work suggesting that there are neurons that encode both positive and negative valence within the rBLA (Zhang et al., 2021), which means both PL and IL could receive signals encoding positive and negative valence from different sources in the BLA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and by inference from the current study's findings.

claim: Subregions of the BLA target distinct networks within the PFC and differentially influence output from PL and IL.
source: Together, our findings delineate how subregions of the BLA target distinct networks within the PFC and differentially influence output from PL and IL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from all experiments in the study.

claim: rBLA and cBLA evoke activity in PL and IL, demonstrating how subregions of the BLA engage distinct cortical networks in the PFC.
source: Together, our findings illustrate how rBLA and cBLA evoke activity in PL and IL, demonstrating how subregions of the BLA engage distinct cortical networks in the PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from all experiments in the study.
